title: The repeated-note arpeggio in 'If You Were Mine'
summary: Hinton asks about Wilson's trademark octave runs; Wilson explains the arpeggio with every other note repeated, inspired by Tatum.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Uh huh. There was one thing that I wanted to ask you which is just so characteristically Teddy Wilson, since we're talking about character. In listening right now, I can't think of anybody else that I've heard do it on the piano -- and the one song that brings to mind is the song, 'If You Were Mine.' Now where did that kind of music -- dee, dee, da, da ... do you know what I'm talking about?
I started to get it, but then I lost it.
Da, da, da, dee, dee ... It's a thing you do with -- it's octave, but it's tremendously effective. Triple octaves. But I don't know of ...
That was inspired by -- it was all inspired by Tatum, because he introduced the running idea -- there's no jazz in that.
But I heard Tatum do that, not only with the -- it's octave, but it's in such good taste. It is so personal, it's Teddy Wilson.
It's really just an arpeggio on the piano, but every other note repeats. That's what it is.
It's one note going up after another one, but every other note is hit twice.
Yeah, it sounds like dee, dee, da, da. Right.
One note and then one in between, and then two, and then one in between. But they all come at the same time. But two of them are hit twice, and then a new note, the next note is hit twice.

If you just shift the notes, with three fingers in your hand, and you shift your hand in place, and start the next three on the last note of the first three, that's what does it, see. One, two, three, and then three, you hit twice and then it becomes one. The last note you play with your little finger, just start the three notes with the thumb. So that note gets hit twice, the little finger hits it and then the thumb hits it. To start the next.
So that automatically gives you two, then one, and then two notes, and they all come at the same time, but two notes repeated.
And another thing, just to wrap it up now ...
It takes a little percussion effect in it.
